title: There's no page one
hookLine: every tractate begins on page two, a reminder that no one starts at the true beginning
carry: nobody starts at the true beginning

cards: You've been meaning to start. Running, writing, an instrument, going back to school, the book you've always wanted to read. But you're waiting for the right beginning.
A Monday. A new notebook. The first of the month.
Everything cleared away so you can start clean, at page one. Here's something strange. Open any tractate of the Babylonian Talmud, in the standard printed editions, and look for page one.
You won't find it. Every single one begins on page two.

teach.h: DAF: A LEAF, SIDES A AND B.
teach.b: A page of Talmud is called a daf. Strictly, a daf is a leaf, with two sides: the front is side a, the back side b. So people cite the Talmud as, say, Berakhot two a: the tractate, the leaf, the side.

teach.h: THE TITLE PAGE WAS PAGE ONE.
teach.b: The usual practical explanation: when the Talmud was printed in Venice five hundred years ago, the first leaf of each volume was the title page.
The text began on the next one, and every later edition kept the same numbering, so a page in one book matches a page in any other, anywhere in the world. But Jewish teachers found a lesson in it.

teach.h: NO ONE STARTS AT THE BEGINNING.
teach.b: There's no page one, they say, because no one ever starts at the true beginning. Before you opened this book, there was the Mishnah; before that, the oral teaching; before that, Sinai.

You're always joining a conversation already underway. And a second lesson, often told in study halls: even when you've finished the whole Talmud, you still haven't mastered the first page. Learning never closes.
Some learners built a whole practice around that idea.

teach.h: DAF YOMI: ONE LEAF A DAY.
teach.b: About a century ago, a rabbi named Meir Shapiro proposed that Jews everywhere learn the same daf each day, one leaf a day. It's called Daf Yomi.
A cycle takes about seven and a half years, and when one ends, the celebrations fill arenas. Then, the next day, they start again.

how: Daf Yomi learners around the world study the same leaf of the Babylonian Talmud each day around the world, and each completed cycle is marked with a celebration called a siyum.

games.q: you've just finished the whole Talmud, one leaf a day, after seven and a half years. the next morning, what do you do?
games.why: Daf Yomi learners celebrate, and the next day begin the cycle again. learning never closes.

practice: Think of the thing you've been waiting to start until conditions are perfect, and let go of the perfect beginning; it was never coming.
Picture starting in the middle of an ordinary day, mess and all: ten minutes, one paragraph, one lap around the block. Hold that small start in mind; it's your page two.
